framing: The index sets the candidate pool for a downstream reranker
paragraphs: A policy search may filter perfectly for a caller and still miss the runbook needed to answer. Exact nearest-neighbor search checks every eligible vector. At the scale used in this chapter, 100 million vectors with 1,536 float32 values each require hundreds of gigabytes before index overhead. Approximate search saves work by skipping candidates.

That shortcut changes a specific part of the system: whether approximate results reproduce the exact vector ranking. HNSW follows graph links, IVF searches selected partitions, and product quantization stores compressed representations. Their settings trade compute, memory, latency, and neighbor recovery. ANN recall measures agreement with exact search. Evaluate whether the embedding captures the user's intent with a task-specific relevance test.

You will trace a tiny HNSW insertion and search, expose an IVF boundary miss as probe depth changes, and budget compressed vector storage. The later examples examine filtering, sharded tail behavior, and replay across metric changes and deletion. Measure recall and latency on each candidate workload, then choose an index family from that frontier.

The production RAG chapter established that retrieval must preserve permission, version, and evidence boundaries. This chapter asks what happens inside its vector search stage. Next, hybrid search adds lexical retrieval alongside dense vectors, because an approximate vector index cannot rescue a code or phrase its embedding ranks poorly.
outcomes: Compare approximate results with an exact baseline at the same metric, filter, and cutoff.
Explain how HNSW search depth or IVF probe count changes work and possible misses.
Evaluate memory, filtered recall, and shard tails before selecting an operating point.
question: How much neighbor recall can your product afford to trade for lower search cost, and how will you measure that boundary?
